posts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
posts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
posts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

posts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
posts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
posts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

posts.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
posts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
posts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

posts.title: Cell-Based Architectures: Designing Fault Isolation Boundaries for Million-User Apps
posts.subtitle: Design and implement cell-based routing using Spring Cloud Gateway to limit system blast radius.
posts.brief: As microservice architectures scale, a single outage in a core service can cascade across the entire system. Cell-Based Architecture mitigates this by partitioning the entire system into small, self-contained, independent units called cells. This guide outlines their routing mechanics and provides a custom Spring Cloud Gateway filter for cell-based traffic distribution.

posts.title: Choosing the Right Database: CAP Theorem and Practical Use Cases
posts.subtitle: Beyond the SQL vs NoSQL debate: A framework for matching database architecture to business requirements.
posts.brief: Database selection is a trade-off between consistency, availability, and scalability. By using the CAP Theorem as a compass and matching your data access patterns to the right storage engine (Relational, Document, KV, or Wide-Column), you can build systems that scale without collapsing under architectural debt.

posts.title: Cloud Architecture Patterns: Cells, Control Planes, Sidecars, and Queue-Based Load Leveling
posts.subtitle: Cloud systems scale by isolating blast radius and separating coordination from request handling.
posts.brief: Cloud scale is not created by sprinkling managed services around a diagram. It comes from isolating failure domains, separating coordination from request serving, and smoothing bursty work before it overloads synchronous paths.

posts.title: The Consistency Continuum: From Read-Your-Own-Writes to Leaderless Replication
posts.subtitle: Beyond 'Strong vs Eventual': Navigating the subtle trade-offs of distributed agreement.
posts.brief: In distributed systems, consistency is a spectrum of trade-offs between latency, availability, and correctness. By leveraging session-based patterns like Read-Your-Own-Writes and formal Quorum logic ($W+R > N$), architects can provide the illusion of strong consistency while maintaining the horizontal scale of eventual consistency.

posts.title: Concurrency Models: Actor Model vs. Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
posts.subtitle: An in-depth mathematical and practical comparison of the Actor Model and CSP concurrency patterns in Java.
posts.brief: Shared-memory multithreading using manual locks is notoriously difficult to scale and debug. To avoid race conditions and deadlocks, modern platforms use message-passing concurrency models. This guide compares the Actor Model (used in Erlang and Akka/Pekko) with Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, used in Go) and provides full Java implementations for both.

posts.title: CosmosDB Partition Internals: Logical vs Physical Partitions Explained
posts.subtitle: How CosmosDB maps your partition key to physical storage — and why the wrong choice costs 10x more at scale
posts.brief:

A retail engineering team ships a flash-sale feature. Traffic spikes 10×. Their Azure CosmosDB bill triples within 24 hours. Queries that ran in 5ms now ta

posts.title: Count-Min Sketch Explained: Frequency Estimation at Streaming Scale
posts.subtitle: How a d × w counter matrix answers 'how often has X appeared?' with a bounded upper bound error and O(1) operations at any stream volume.
posts.brief: Count-Min Sketch (CMS) is a fixed-size `d × w` counter matrix that estimates how often any element has appeared in a stream. Insert: hash the element with each of the `d` hash functions to get one column per row, increment those `d` counters. Query: read the same `d` counters, return the **minimum** — an upper bound that is never an underestimate. With `d = 7` rows and `w = 2000` columns, a ~112 KB sketch delivers <1% error for hashtag frequency estimation across millions of events — versus gigabytes for exact counting. Twitter trending topics, Akamai heavy-hitter detection, and Apache Flink streaming analytics all use Count-Min Sketch.

posts.title: CQRS Pattern: Separating Write Models from Query Models at Scale
posts.subtitle: Design independent command and query paths to scale reads without weakening write correctness.
posts.brief: CQRS works when read and write workloads diverge, but only with explicit freshness budgets and projection reliability. The hard part is not separating models — it is operating lag, replay, and rollback safely.

posts.title: Dense LLM Architecture: How Every Parameter Works on Every Token
posts.subtitle: Inside the dense transformer block — attention heads, FFN layers, and why scaling dense models hits a wall
posts.brief: In a dense LLM every single parameter is active for every token in every forward pass — no routing, no selection. A transformer block runs multi-head self-attention (Q, K, V) followed by a feed-forward network (FFN) with roughly 4× the hidden dimension. Stack 32–96 of those blocks and you have GPT-3, LLaMA-2, or Mistral. The compute cost scales with the product of parameters and tokens, which is why models like Mixtral replaced dense layers with Mixture-of-Experts routing.

posts.title: Dot Product in Machine Learning: The Engine Behind Similarity, Attention, and Neural Networks
posts.subtitle: From cosine similarity to scaled dot-product attention — how one operation powers modern AI
posts.brief: The dot product multiplies corresponding elements of two vectors and sums the results. In machine learning it does three critical jobs: it scores semantic similarity between embeddings, computes every activation in a fully connected layer, and generates the Q·Kᵀ score matrix that transformer attention uses to decide what to focus on. Normalising by vector magnitude turns it into cosine similarity; dividing by √d_k in attention prevents softmax saturation. Master this one operation and the internals of neural networks, transformers, and vector search all click into place.

posts.title: The Dual Write Problem in NoSQL: MongoDB, DynamoDB, and Cassandra
posts.subtitle: Why NoSQL consistency is harder than you think — and the per-database patterns that fix it
posts.brief: NoSQL databases trade cross-entity atomicity for scale — and every database draws that atomicity boundary in a different place. MongoDB's boundary is the document (pre-4.0) or the replica set (4.0+ multi-doc transactions). DynamoDB's boundary is a single `TransactWriteItems` call, with failure modes that silently burn throughput. Cassandra's boundary is the partition key. Write across any of these boundaries without a compensating pattern — Outbox, CDC, or conditional writes — and you will have silent data divergence in production.

posts.title: System Design: Designing an Autonomous AI Coding Agent (Devin at Scale)
posts.subtitle: Learn how to design a secure, isolated, and scalable high-level system for an autonomous AI software engineer at enterprise scale.
posts.brief: Designing an autonomous AI coding agent at scale is not a prompt engineering task; it is a complex systems problem. The system requires secure multitenancy via Firecracker microVMs, a low-latency workspace syncing event loop, and a dual planning-execution engine backed by durable state to survive compile-and-retry loops.

posts.title: How Kafka Works: The Log That Never Forgets
posts.subtitle: Kafka is not just a message queue; it's a distributed streaming platform. We explain Topics, Partitions, and Offsets.
posts.brief: Kafka is a distributed event store. Unlike a traditional queue (RabbitMQ) where messages disappear after reading, Kafka stores them in a persistent **Log**. This allows multiple consumers to read the same data at their own pace, replay history, and handle massive scale via **Partitions**.

posts.title: ID Generation Strategies in System Design: Base62, UUID, Snowflake, and Beyond
posts.subtitle: How to choose the right uniqueness strategy — from 6-char short URLs to distributed int64 order IDs
posts.brief: Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.

posts.title: Large Language Models (LLMs): The Generative AI Revolution
posts.subtitle: From GPT-3 to GPT-4. How scaling up simple text prediction created emergent intelligence.
posts.brief: Large Language Models predict the next token, one at a time, using a Transformer architecture trained on billions of words. At scale, this simple objective produces emergent reasoning, coding, and world-model capabilities. Understanding the training pipeline (pre-training → instruction tuning → RLHF), how attention works, and where LLMs fail is the baseline for any serious LLM engineering work.

posts.title: LLD for URL Shortener: Designing TinyURL
posts.subtitle: How do you turn a long URL into a 7-character string? We explore Base62 encoding, Hash collisions, and database choices.
posts.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: A URL Shortener maps long URLs to short IDs. The core challenge is generating a globally unique, short, collision-free ID at scale. We use Base62 encoding on auto-incrementing database IDs

posts.title: LLM Hyperparameters Guide: Temperature, Top-P, and Top-K Explained
posts.subtitle: Why does ChatGPT sometimes write poetry and sometimes write code? It's all in the settings. We explain how to tune LLMs for creativity vs. precision.
posts.brief: Temperature, Top-p, and Top-k are three sampling controls that determine how "creative" or "deterministic" an LLM's output is. Temperature rescales the probability distribution; Top-k limits the candidate pool by count; Top-p limits it by cumulative probability. Understanding all three — and when to combine them — is essential for production LLM work.

posts.title: What are Logits in Machine Learning and Why They Matter
posts.subtitle: Logits are the raw, unnormalized scores output by a neural network before they are turned into pr...
posts.brief: Logits are the raw, unnormalized scores produced by the final layer of a neural network — before any probability transformation. Softmax converts them to probabilities. Temperature scales them before Softmax to control output randomness.

posts.title: Modern Table Formats: Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg vs Apache Hudi
posts.subtitle: Parquet alone breaks at scale: Delta Lake, Iceberg, and Hudi bring ACID, time travel, and schema evolution to object storage.
posts.brief: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi are open table formats that wrap Parquet files with a transaction log (or snapshot tree) to deliver ACID guarantees, time travel, schema evolution, and efficient upserts on object storage. Choose Delta Lake for Databricks/Spark-centric shops, Iceberg for multi-engine portability at petabyte scale, and Hudi for near-real-time CDC upserts and streaming pipelines.

posts.title: Modernization Architecture Patterns: Strangler Fig, Anti-Corruption Layers, and Modular Monoliths
posts.subtitle: Move legacy systems safely by carving seams, translating contracts, and reducing rewrite risk.
posts.brief: Large-scale modernization usually fails when teams try to replace an entire legacy platform in one synchronized rewrite. The safer approach is to create seams, translate old contracts into stable new ones, and move traffic gradually with measurable rollback points.

posts.title: NoSQL Partitioning: How Cassandra, DynamoDB, and MongoDB Split Data
posts.subtitle: Consistent hashing rings, adaptive capacity, and chunk balancers — how the three leading NoSQL databases partition data at scale
posts.brief: Every NoSQL database hides a partitioning engine behind a deceptively simple API. Cassandra uses a consistent hashing ring where a Murmur3 hash of your partition key selects a node — virtual nodes (vnodes) make rebalancing smooth. DynamoDB manages partitioning completely on your behalf, splitting physical partitions at 10 GB automatically and redistributing throughput via adaptive capacity — but a structurally hot partition key still requires write sharding at the application layer. MongoDB divides collections into chunks routed by a `mongos` process, with ranged shard keys enabling efficient range queries and hashed shard keys distributing writes uniformly; jumbo chunks signal a low-cardinality shard key. In all three systems, the partition key decision is permanent and architectural — getting it wrong is a 2 AM production incident, not a config file change.

posts.title: PagedAttention & KV-Cache Optimization: How vLLM Handles Large Scale Inference
posts.subtitle: How virtual memory paged block mapping solves GPU memory bottleneck and fragmentation in LLM inference.
posts.brief: Large Language Model (LLM) serving is heavily bound by GPU memory capacity due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Traditional serving frameworks allocate contiguous memory based on maximum sequence length, leading to severe fragmentation and wasted space. This guide explores how PagedAttention, inspired by operating system virtual memory, partitions the KV cache into small logical blocks to enable dynamic, non-contiguous allocations, prefix sharing, and massive throughput gains.

posts.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
posts.subtitle: Trade exact answers for fixed memory and O(1) operations: a comparative guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch.
posts.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

posts.title: Serverless Architecture Pattern: Event-Driven Scale with Operational Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Use functions and managed triggers for bursty workloads while controlling latency and vendor coupling.
posts.brief: Serverless is strongest for spiky asynchronous workloads when cold-start, observability, and state boundaries are intentionally designed.

posts.title: Softmax Function Explained: From Raw Scores to Probabilities
posts.subtitle: Why every neural network classifier converts its raw output through exponential normalization before calling it a prediction
posts.brief: Softmax converts a vector of raw scores (logits) into a valid probability distribution by exponentiating each value and dividing by the total. Subtracting the max before exponentiating prevents floating-point overflow. Temperature scaling controls how "peaked" or "flat" the distribution is. Softmax appears twice in every transformer — inside scaled dot-product attention and at the vocabulary output head — making it one of the most consequential two-line functions in all of deep learning.

posts.title: Spark on Kubernetes: Operator, Dynamic Allocation, and Production Monitoring
posts.subtitle: How Spark runs on Kubernetes using the Spark Operator, Dynamic Resource Allocation, pod templates, and Prometheus metrics for production observability
posts.brief: Running Spark on Kubernetes replaces YARN's static queue model with a container-native, elastically-scaled execution environment. The kubeflow Spark Operator manages SparkApplication CRDs through a reconciliation loop that creates driver and executor pods, while Dynamic Resource Allocation and pod templates give platform teams granular control over where pods land and how resources are consumed. Prometheus ServiceMonitors expose executor-level metrics that YARN never surfaced, and proper memoryOverhead tuning is the single most common gap between a demo and a stable production deployment.

posts.title: Partitioning in Spark: HashPartitioner, RangePartitioner, and Custom Strategies
posts.subtitle: Partition count and strategy determine whether your Spark job scales linearly or falls apart at 10x data — here is what happens under the hood
posts.brief: Spark's partition count and partitioning strategy are the two levers that determine whether a job scales linearly or crumbles under data growth. HashPartitioner distributes keys by hash modulo — fast and uniform for well-distributed keys, catastrophic for hot keys. RangePartitioner samples the dataset to find natural boundaries, preserving sort order at the cost of an extra pass. Custom partitioners route by domain logic when neither built-in strategy fits. Diagnosing skew in the Spark UI stage detail view — not guessing at `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` — is the only reliable path to the right fix.

posts.title: Reading and Writing Data in Spark: Parquet, Delta, JSON, and JDBC
posts.subtitle: The format you choose for Spark I/O determines whether predicate pushdown saves you 90% of a scan or reads every byte
posts.brief: Parquet's columnar layout with row-group statistics enables predicate pushdown that can reduce a 500 GB scan to 8 GB. Delta Lake wraps Parquet with a JSON transaction log to add ACID semantics and time travel. JSON and CSV read every byte because they have no statistics. JDBC reads scale only with explicit `numPartitions` + `partitionColumn`. The format you choose is not cosmetic — it determines the entire I/O path before a single task runs.

posts.title: Sparse Mixture of Experts: How MoE LLMs Do More With Less Compute
posts.subtitle: How MoE replaces the dense FFN with N expert layers and a learned router — GPT-4-scale capacity at a fraction of inference cost
posts.brief: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces the single dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in each Transformer block with **N independent expert FFNs** plus a **learned router**. Only the top-K experts activate per token — so total parameters far exceed active parameters. Mixtral 8×7B carries 47B total parameters but computes like a ~12.9B model per forward pass. GPT-4 is widely believed to use a similar architecture at much larger scale. The payoff: near-GPT-4-quality output at GPT-3.5-level inference cost.

posts.title: System Design API Design for Interviews: Contracts, Idempotency, and Pagination
posts.subtitle: Design APIs interviewers trust by focusing on resource boundaries, request contracts, and failure-safe behavior.
posts.brief: In system design interviews, API design is not a list of HTTP verbs. It is a contract strategy: clear resource boundaries, stable request and response shapes, pagination, idempotency, error semantics, and versioning decisions that survive scale and failures.

posts.title: System Design: Complete Guide to Caching — Patterns, Eviction, and Distributed Strategies
posts.subtitle: Cache-Aside to Refresh-Ahead, LRU to ARC — every caching pattern, eviction policy, and distributed strategy you need for system design
posts.brief: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

posts.title: System Design Data Modeling and Schema Evolution: Query-Driven Storage That Survives Change
posts.subtitle: Learn how to choose entities, indexes, and schema evolution strategies that match real query patterns at scale.
posts.brief: In system design interviews, data modeling is where architecture meets reality. A good model starts from query patterns, chooses clear entity boundaries, defines indexes deliberately, and includes a schema evolution path so the system can change without breaking reads and writes.

posts.title: System Design Databases: SQL vs NoSQL and Scaling
posts.subtitle: The eternal debate: SQL or NoSQL? We break down ACID vs BASE, Sharding vs Replication, and when to use MongoDB vs PostgreSQL.
posts.brief: SQL gives you ACID guarantees and powerful relational queries; NoSQL gives you horizontal scale and flexible schemas. The real decision is not "which is better" — it is "which trade-offs align with your workload." Understanding replication, sharding, and the CAP theorem helps you pick correctly every time.

posts.title: System Design: Designing a Financial Ledger with Double-Entry Constraints
posts.subtitle: How to design a highly consistent, idempotent, and auditable double-entry bookkeeping ledger at scale.
posts.brief: Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies without sacrificing transactional guarantees.

posts.title: High-Level Design: Building a Real-Time Ad Click Aggregator at Scale
posts.subtitle: Design a high-throughput real-time stream aggregation system that processes billions of events with exactly-once guarantees.
posts.brief: Scaling an ad click aggregator requires processing massive event streams (billions of clicks per day) with exactly-once delivery guarantees. We achieve this using Kafka-based event ingestion, Apache Flink stateful stream aggregation, and timeseries databases.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Distributed Cache Platform
posts.subtitle: Interview HLD for a distributed cache with eviction, invalidation, and resilience trade-offs.
posts.brief: Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: E-Commerce Platform (Amazon)
posts.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a large-scale e-commerce system handling catalog, cart, inventory, and orders.
posts.brief: A large-scale e-commerce platform separates catalog, cart, inventory, orders, and payments into independent microservices. The core architectural challenge is **Inventory Correctness** during flash sales—solved with a two-phase reservation pattern: an atomic Redis `DECR` for high-speed "soft" reservation and an optimistic-lock SQL update for the final "hard" commitment.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Real-Time Leaderboard
posts.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a real-time gaming leaderboard with fast rank queries.
posts.brief: Real-time leaderboards for 10M+ active users require an in-memory ranking engine. **Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET)** are the industry standard, providing $O(\log N)$ updates and rank lookups via an internal **Skip List** data structure. Relational databases fail at this scale because calculating rank is an $O(N)$ operation (counting rows with higher scores) that becomes a bottleneck during peak traffic spikes.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Search Autocomplete (Google/Amazon)
posts.subtitle: Sub-10ms prefix lookup, ranking, typo tolerance, and language-partitioned indexes at Google scale.
posts.brief: Search autocomplete must respond in sub-10ms to feel "instant." The core trade-off is **Latency vs. Data Freshness**: we use an offline pipeline (Spark) to pre-calculate prefix-to-suggestion mappings and store them in **Redis Sorted Sets** (or a specialized Trie) for near-instant retrieval, while sacrificing real-time updates for most queries.

posts.title: High-Level Design: Scaling a Concert Ticket Booking System under Flash Load
posts.subtitle: Design a scalable concert ticket booking system that handles massive traffic surges and prevents double-booking.
posts.brief: Designing a high-scale ticket booking system requires balancing high read traffic (seat map lookups) with extreme write concurrency (seat lock attempts) during popular concert drops. We achieve this using Redis-based temporary ticket locks and distributed queues.

posts.title: Microservices Architecture: Decomposition, Communication, and Trade-offs
posts.subtitle: When microservices help, when they hurt, and how to decompose a monolith the right way.
posts.brief: Microservices let teams deploy and scale services independently — but every service boundary you draw costs you a network hop, a consistency challenge, and an operational burden. The architecture pays off only when your team and traffic scale have genuinely outgrown a well-structured monolith.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Web Crawler
posts.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a distributed web crawler handling politeness, deduplication, and scale.
posts.brief: A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the stability of the target websites.

posts.title: System Design Interview Basics: A Beginner-Friendly Framework for Clear Answers
posts.subtitle: A beginner-friendly way to structure requirements, estimates, diagrams, and trade-offs in your first design round.
posts.brief: System design interviews are not about inventing a perfect architecture on the spot. They are about showing a calm, repeatable process: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a simple design, explain trade-offs, and improve it when constraints change.

posts.title: System Design Sharding Strategy: Choosing Keys, Avoiding Hot Spots, and Resharding Safely
posts.subtitle: A practical guide to shard keys, routing, hot partitions, and how to scale storage without breaking queries.
posts.brief: Sharding means splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical databases so no single node carries all the data and traffic. The hard part is not adding more nodes. The hard part is choosing a shard key that keeps data balanced and queries practical.

posts.title: The Ultimate Data Structures Cheat Sheet
posts.subtitle: A practical cheat sheet for choosing the right data structure based on access pattern, scale, and performance goals.
posts.brief: Data structures are tools. Picking the right one depends on what operation you do most: lookup, insert, delete, ordered traversal, top-k, prefix search, or graph navigation. Start from operation frequency, not from habit.

posts.title: The Ultimate Guide to Acing the System Design Interview
posts.subtitle: Don't panic. System Design interviews are open-ended discussions. This framework (Requirements, API, DB, Scale) will help you structure your answer.
posts.brief: System Design interviews are collaborative whiteboard sessions, not trick-question coding tests. Follow the framework — Requirements → Estimations → API → Data Model → High-Level Architecture → Deep-Dive — and you turn vague product ideas into defensible, production-ready designs.

posts.title: Write-Time vs Read-Time Fan-Out: How Social Feeds Scale
posts.subtitle: The celebrity threshold, Redis sorted sets, and the hybrid model every social platform actually ships.
posts.brief: Fan-out is the act of distributing one post to many followers' feeds. Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes feeds at post time — fast reads but catastrophic write amplification for celebrities. Read-time fan-out (pull) computes feeds on demand — no amplification but slow reads at scale. Production systems like Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook use a **hybrid**: write-time fan-out for users with ≤ 10K followers, read-time fan-out injected at read for celebrities above that threshold.

posts.title: SAGA Pattern Compensations
posts.subtitle: Maintain eventual consistency across microservices with compensating transactions instead of 2PC.
posts.brief: In distributed systems, committing transactions across multiple database nodes with Two-Phase Commit (2PC) blocks resources and limits scale. The SAGA pattern solves this by executing a series of loca

posts.brief: Websites under stress

posts.title: What happens when a database gets too big for one server? | Database Sharding & Partitioning
posts.subtitle: Master database sharding and partitioning to scale your data infrastructure horizontally and overcome single-server limitations.
posts.brief: When a single database server hits its limits, sharding and partitioning offer powerful strategies to scale.

posts.title: How to serve data at lightning speed | Caching Strategies (Redis/Memcached)
posts.subtitle: Unlock blazing-fast data delivery and drastically reduce database load with advanced caching strategies using Redis and Memcached.
posts.brief: Master caching to accelerate data access, improve system responsiveness, and scale efficiently.

posts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
posts.subtitle: From WAL and MVCC to fsync and isolation levels — the internals behind every ACID guarantee in PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
posts.brief: ACID is four orthogonal guarantees that every SQL transaction must provide. Atomicity says all-or-nothing: PostgreSQL implements it via WAL rollback; MySQL InnoDB via undo logs. Consistency says constraints always hold: the database rejects any write that violates a `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`, or `NOT NULL`. Isolation says concurrent transactions cannot see each other's intermediate states: PostgreSQL uses MVCC + Serializable Snapshot Isolation; MySQL InnoDB uses MVCC + Two-Phase Locking. Durability says committed data survives crashes: every major database writes to a write-ahead log and calls `fsync` before acknowledging a commit. Know which property protects which failure class — and know the configuration knobs that let you trade durability for throughput when the workload permits.

posts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
posts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
posts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

posts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
posts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
posts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

posts.title: Advanced AI: Agents, RAG, and the Future of Intelligence
posts.subtitle: Is an LLM a brain in a jar? To make it truly useful, we need to give it access to the world. This guide explains RAG and Agents.
posts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

posts.title: Advanced Graph Algorithms: Dijkstra, Topological Sort, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU)
posts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
posts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

posts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
posts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
posts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

posts.title: AI Architecture Patterns: Routers, Planner-Worker Loops, Memory Layers, and Evaluation Guardrails
posts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
posts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

journey.label: Scale
journey.description: Learn Scale as a connected topic across chapters, concepts, simulations, and interview reasoning.

articles.title: How do websites survive unexpected traffic spikes? | Load Balancing Explained
articles.brief: Websites under stress

articles.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
articles.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

articles.title: Count-Min Sketch Explained: Frequency Estimation at Streaming Scale
articles.brief: Count-Min Sketch (CMS) is a fixed-size `d × w` counter matrix that estimates how often any element has appeared in a stream. Insert: hash the element with each of the `d` hash functions to get one column per row, increment those `d` counters. Query: read the same `d` counters, return the **minimum** — an upper bound that is never an underestimate. With `d = 7` rows and `w = 2000` columns, a ~112 KB sketch delivers <1% error for hashtag frequency estimation across millions of events — versus gigabytes for exact counting. Twitter trending topics, Akamai heavy-hitter detection, and Apache Flink streaming analytics all use Count-Min Sketch.

articles.title: CQRS Pattern: Separating Write Models from Query Models at Scale
articles.brief: CQRS works when read and write workloads diverge, but only with explicit freshness budgets and projection reliability. The hard part is not separating models — it is operating lag, replay, and rollback safely.

articles.title: System Design: Designing an Autonomous AI Coding Agent (Devin at Scale)
articles.brief: Designing an autonomous AI coding agent at scale is not a prompt engineering task; it is a complex systems problem. The system requires secure multitenancy via Firecracker microVMs, a low-latency workspace syncing event loop, and a dual planning-execution engine backed by durable state to survive compile-and-retry loops.

articles.title: PagedAttention & KV-Cache Optimization: How vLLM Handles Large Scale Inference
articles.brief: Large Language Model (LLM) serving is heavily bound by GPU memory capacity due to the Key-Value (KV) cache. Traditional serving frameworks allocate contiguous memory based on maximum sequence length, leading to severe fragmentation and wasted space. This guide explores how PagedAttention, inspired by operating system virtual memory, partitions the KV cache into small logical blocks to enable dynamic, non-contiguous allocations, prefix sharing, and massive throughput gains.

articles.title: Serverless Architecture Pattern: Event-Driven Scale with Operational Guardrails
articles.brief: Serverless is strongest for spiky asynchronous workloads when cold-start, observability, and state boundaries are intentionally designed.

articles.title: High-Level Design: Building a Real-Time Ad Click Aggregator at Scale
articles.brief: Scaling an ad click aggregator requires processing massive event streams (billions of clicks per day) with exactly-once delivery guarantees. We achieve this using Kafka-based event ingestion, Apache Flink stateful stream aggregation, and timeseries databases.

articles.title: Write-Time vs Read-Time Fan-Out: How Social Feeds Scale
articles.brief: Fan-out is the act of distributing one post to many followers' feeds. Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes feeds at post time — fast reads but catastrophic write amplification for celebrities. Read-time fan-out (pull) computes feeds on demand — no amplification but slow reads at scale. Production systems like Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook use a **hybrid**: write-time fan-out for users with ≤ 10K followers, read-time fan-out injected at read for celebrities above that threshold.

articles.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
articles.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

articles.title: Big Data Architecture Patterns: Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh
articles.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

articles.title: Cell-Based Architectures: Designing Fault Isolation Boundaries for Million-User Apps
articles.brief: As microservice architectures scale, a single outage in a core service can cascade across the entire system. Cell-Based Architecture mitigates this by partitioning the entire system into small, self-contained, independent units called cells. This guide outlines their routing mechanics and provides a custom Spring Cloud Gateway filter for cell-based traffic distribution.

articles.title: Choosing the Right Database: CAP Theorem and Practical Use Cases
articles.brief: Database selection is a trade-off between consistency, availability, and scalability. By using the CAP Theorem as a compass and matching your data access patterns to the right storage engine (Relational, Document, KV, or Wide-Column), you can build systems that scale without collapsing under architectural debt.

articles.title: Cloud Architecture Patterns: Cells, Control Planes, Sidecars, and Queue-Based Load Leveling
articles.brief: Cloud scale is not created by sprinkling managed services around a diagram. It comes from isolating failure domains, separating coordination from request serving, and smoothing bursty work before it overloads synchronous paths.

articles.title: The Consistency Continuum: From Read-Your-Own-Writes to Leaderless Replication
articles.brief: In distributed systems, consistency is a spectrum of trade-offs between latency, availability, and correctness. By leveraging session-based patterns like Read-Your-Own-Writes and formal Quorum logic ($W+R > N$), architects can provide the illusion of strong consistency while maintaining the horizontal scale of eventual consistency.

articles.title: Concurrency Models: Actor Model vs. Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP)
articles.brief: Shared-memory multithreading using manual locks is notoriously difficult to scale and debug. To avoid race conditions and deadlocks, modern platforms use message-passing concurrency models. This guide compares the Actor Model (used in Erlang and Akka/Pekko) with Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP, used in Go) and provides full Java implementations for both.

articles.title: CosmosDB Partition Internals: Logical vs Physical Partitions Explained
articles.brief:
🔥 When Your Database Bill Triples Overnight
A retail engineering team ships a flash-sale feature. Traffic spikes 10×. Their Azure CosmosDB bill triples within 24 hours. Queries that ran in 5ms now ta

articles.title: Dense LLM Architecture: How Every Parameter Works on Every Token
articles.brief: In a dense LLM every single parameter is active for every token in every forward pass — no routing, no selection. A transformer block runs multi-head self-attention (Q, K, V) followed by a feed-forward network (FFN) with roughly 4× the hidden dimension. Stack 32–96 of those blocks and you have GPT-3, LLaMA-2, or Mistral. The compute cost scales with the product of parameters and tokens, which is why models like Mixtral replaced dense layers with Mixture-of-Experts routing.

articles.title: Dot Product in Machine Learning: The Engine Behind Similarity, Attention, and Neural Networks
articles.brief: The dot product multiplies corresponding elements of two vectors and sums the results. In machine learning it does three critical jobs: it scores semantic similarity between embeddings, computes every activation in a fully connected layer, and generates the Q·Kᵀ score matrix that transformer attention uses to decide what to focus on. Normalising by vector magnitude turns it into cosine similarity; dividing by √d_k in attention prevents softmax saturation. Master this one operation and the internals of neural networks, transformers, and vector search all click into place.

articles.title: The Dual Write Problem in NoSQL: MongoDB, DynamoDB, and Cassandra
articles.brief: NoSQL databases trade cross-entity atomicity for scale — and every database draws that atomicity boundary in a different place. MongoDB's boundary is the document (pre-4.0) or the replica set (4.0+ multi-doc transactions). DynamoDB's boundary is a single `TransactWriteItems` call, with failure modes that silently burn throughput. Cassandra's boundary is the partition key. Write across any of these boundaries without a compensating pattern — Outbox, CDC, or conditional writes — and you will have silent data divergence in production.
articles.primaryConcept: The Dual Write Problem in NoSQL

articles.title: How Kafka Works: The Log That Never Forgets
articles.brief: Kafka is a distributed event store. Unlike a traditional queue (RabbitMQ) where messages disappear after reading, Kafka stores them in a persistent **Log**. This allows multiple consumers to read the same data at their own pace, replay history, and handle massive scale via **Partitions**.

articles.title: ID Generation Strategies in System Design: Base62, UUID, Snowflake, and Beyond
articles.brief: Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.
articles.primaryConcept: ID Generation Strategies in System Design

articles.title: Large Language Models (LLMs): The Generative AI Revolution
articles.brief: Large Language Models predict the next token, one at a time, using a Transformer architecture trained on billions of words. At scale, this simple objective produces emergent reasoning, coding, and world-model capabilities. Understanding the training pipeline (pre-training → instruction tuning → RLHF), how attention works, and where LLMs fail is the baseline for any serious LLM engineering work.

articles.title: LLD for URL Shortener: Designing TinyURL
articles.brief:
TLDR

TLDR: A URL Shortener maps long URLs to short IDs. The core challenge is generating a globally unique, short, collision-free ID at scale. We use Base62 encoding on auto-incrementing database IDs

articles.title: LLM Hyperparameters Guide: Temperature, Top-P, and Top-K Explained
articles.brief: Temperature, Top-p, and Top-k are three sampling controls that determine how "creative" or "deterministic" an LLM's output is. Temperature rescales the probability distribution; Top-k limits the candidate pool by count; Top-p limits it by cumulative probability. Understanding all three — and when to combine them — is essential for production LLM work.

articles.title: What are Logits in Machine Learning and Why They Matter
articles.brief: Logits are the raw, unnormalized scores produced by the final layer of a neural network — before any probability transformation. Softmax converts them to probabilities. Temperature scales them before Softmax to control output randomness.

articles.title: Modern Table Formats: Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg vs Apache Hudi
articles.brief: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and Apache Hudi are open table formats that wrap Parquet files with a transaction log (or snapshot tree) to deliver ACID guarantees, time travel, schema evolution, and efficient upserts on object storage. Choose Delta Lake for Databricks/Spark-centric shops, Iceberg for multi-engine portability at petabyte scale, and Hudi for near-real-time CDC upserts and streaming pipelines.

articles.title: Modernization Architecture Patterns: Strangler Fig, Anti-Corruption Layers, and Modular Monoliths
articles.brief: Large-scale modernization usually fails when teams try to replace an entire legacy platform in one synchronized rewrite. The safer approach is to create seams, translate old contracts into stable new ones, and move traffic gradually with measurable rollback points.

articles.title: NoSQL Partitioning: How Cassandra, DynamoDB, and MongoDB Split Data
articles.brief: Every NoSQL database hides a partitioning engine behind a deceptively simple API. Cassandra uses a consistent hashing ring where a Murmur3 hash of your partition key selects a node — virtual nodes (vnodes) make rebalancing smooth. DynamoDB manages partitioning completely on your behalf, splitting physical partitions at 10 GB automatically and redistributing throughput via adaptive capacity — but a structurally hot partition key still requires write sharding at the application layer. MongoDB divides collections into chunks routed by a `mongos` process, with ranged shard keys enabling efficient range queries and hashed shard keys distributing writes uniformly; jumbo chunks signal a low-cardinality shard key. In all three systems, the partition key decision is permanent and architectural — getting it wrong is a 2 AM production incident, not a config file change.

articles.title: Probabilistic Data Structures: A Practical Guide to Bloom Filters, HyperLogLog, and Count-Min Sketch
articles.brief: Probabilistic data structures trade a small, bounded probability of being wrong for orders-of-magnitude better memory efficiency and O(1) speed. Bloom Filters answer "definitely not in this set" in constant time with zero false negatives. HyperLogLog counts billions of unique elements in 12 KB with ±0.81% error. Count-Min Sketch estimates how often any element appeared in a stream using a fixed counter matrix. Each structure solves a different question — membership, cardinality, or frequency — at scales where exact answers are unaffordable.

articles.title: Softmax Function Explained: From Raw Scores to Probabilities
articles.brief: Softmax converts a vector of raw scores (logits) into a valid probability distribution by exponentiating each value and dividing by the total. Subtracting the max before exponentiating prevents floating-point overflow. Temperature scaling controls how "peaked" or "flat" the distribution is. Softmax appears twice in every transformer — inside scaled dot-product attention and at the vocabulary output head — making it one of the most consequential two-line functions in all of deep learning.

articles.title: Spark on Kubernetes: Operator, Dynamic Allocation, and Production Monitoring
articles.brief: Running Spark on Kubernetes replaces YARN's static queue model with a container-native, elastically-scaled execution environment. The kubeflow Spark Operator manages SparkApplication CRDs through a reconciliation loop that creates driver and executor pods, while Dynamic Resource Allocation and pod templates give platform teams granular control over where pods land and how resources are consumed. Prometheus ServiceMonitors expose executor-level metrics that YARN never surfaced, and proper memoryOverhead tuning is the single most common gap between a demo and a stable production deployment.

articles.title: Partitioning in Spark: HashPartitioner, RangePartitioner, and Custom Strategies
articles.brief: Spark's partition count and partitioning strategy are the two levers that determine whether a job scales linearly or crumbles under data growth. HashPartitioner distributes keys by hash modulo — fast and uniform for well-distributed keys, catastrophic for hot keys. RangePartitioner samples the dataset to find natural boundaries, preserving sort order at the cost of an extra pass. Custom partitioners route by domain logic when neither built-in strategy fits. Diagnosing skew in the Spark UI stage detail view — not guessing at `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` — is the only reliable path to the right fix.

articles.title: Reading and Writing Data in Spark: Parquet, Delta, JSON, and JDBC
articles.brief: Parquet's columnar layout with row-group statistics enables predicate pushdown that can reduce a 500 GB scan to 8 GB. Delta Lake wraps Parquet with a JSON transaction log to add ACID semantics and time travel. JSON and CSV read every byte because they have no statistics. JDBC reads scale only with explicit `numPartitions` + `partitionColumn`. The format you choose is not cosmetic — it determines the entire I/O path before a single task runs.
articles.primaryConcept: Reading and Writing Data in Spark

articles.title: Sparse Mixture of Experts: How MoE LLMs Do More With Less Compute
articles.brief: Mixture of Experts (MoE) replaces the single dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layer in each Transformer block with **N independent expert FFNs** plus a **learned router**. Only the top-K experts activate per token — so total parameters far exceed active parameters. Mixtral 8×7B carries 47B total parameters but computes like a ~12.9B model per forward pass. GPT-4 is widely believed to use a similar architecture at much larger scale. The payoff: near-GPT-4-quality output at GPT-3.5-level inference cost.

articles.title: System Design API Design for Interviews: Contracts, Idempotency, and Pagination
articles.brief: In system design interviews, API design is not a list of HTTP verbs. It is a contract strategy: clear resource boundaries, stable request and response shapes, pagination, idempotency, error semantics, and versioning decisions that survive scale and failures.
articles.primaryConcept: System Design API Design for Interviews

articles.title: System Design: Complete Guide to Caching — Patterns, Eviction, and Distributed Strategies
articles.brief: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

articles.title: System Design Data Modeling and Schema Evolution: Query-Driven Storage That Survives Change
articles.brief: In system design interviews, data modeling is where architecture meets reality. A good model starts from query patterns, chooses clear entity boundaries, defines indexes deliberately, and includes a schema evolution path so the system can change without breaking reads and writes.
articles.primaryConcept: System Design Data Modeling and Schema Evolution

articles.title: System Design Databases: SQL vs NoSQL and Scaling
articles.brief: SQL gives you ACID guarantees and powerful relational queries; NoSQL gives you horizontal scale and flexible schemas. The real decision is not "which is better" — it is "which trade-offs align with your workload." Understanding replication, sharding, and the CAP theorem helps you pick correctly every time.

articles.title: System Design: Designing a Financial Ledger with Double-Entry Constraints
articles.brief: Designing a financial ledger requires strict double-entry compliance, high consistency, and complete auditability. Unlike traditional databases where records are updated in-place, a financial ledger must be append-only to preserve a verifiable transaction history. This guide details how to architect a scalable ledger system using relational storage, idempotency mechanisms, and active-active isolation strategies without sacrificing transactional guarantees.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Distributed Cache Platform
articles.brief: Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: E-Commerce Platform (Amazon)
articles.brief: A large-scale e-commerce platform separates catalog, cart, inventory, orders, and payments into independent microservices. The core architectural challenge is **Inventory Correctness** during flash sales—solved with a two-phase reservation pattern: an atomic Redis `DECR` for high-speed "soft" reservation and an optimistic-lock SQL update for the final "hard" commitment.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Real-Time Leaderboard
articles.brief: Real-time leaderboards for 10M+ active users require an in-memory ranking engine. **Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET)** are the industry standard, providing $O(\log N)$ updates and rank lookups via an internal **Skip List** data structure. Relational databases fail at this scale because calculating rank is an $O(N)$ operation (counting rows with higher scores) that becomes a bottleneck during peak traffic spikes.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Search Autocomplete (Google/Amazon)
articles.brief: Search autocomplete must respond in sub-10ms to feel "instant." The core trade-off is **Latency vs. Data Freshness**: we use an offline pipeline (Spark) to pre-calculate prefix-to-suggestion mappings and store them in **Redis Sorted Sets** (or a specialized Trie) for near-instant retrieval, while sacrificing real-time updates for most queries.

articles.title: High-Level Design: Scaling a Concert Ticket Booking System under Flash Load
articles.brief: Designing a high-scale ticket booking system requires balancing high read traffic (seat map lookups) with extreme write concurrency (seat lock attempts) during popular concert drops. We achieve this using Redis-based temporary ticket locks and distributed queues.

articles.title: Microservices Architecture: Decomposition, Communication, and Trade-offs
articles.brief: Microservices let teams deploy and scale services independently — but every service boundary you draw costs you a network hop, a consistency challenge, and an operational burden. The architecture pays off only when your team and traffic scale have genuinely outgrown a well-structured monolith.

articles.title: System Design HLD Example: Web Crawler
articles.brief: A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the stability of the target websites.

articles.title: System Design Interview Basics: A Beginner-Friendly Framework for Clear Answers
articles.brief: System design interviews are not about inventing a perfect architecture on the spot. They are about showing a calm, repeatable process: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a simple design, explain trade-offs, and improve it when constraints change.

articles.title: System Design Sharding Strategy: Choosing Keys, Avoiding Hot Spots, and Resharding Safely
articles.brief: Sharding means splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical databases so no single node carries all the data and traffic. The hard part is not adding more nodes. The hard part is choosing a shard key that keeps data balanced and queries practical.

articles.title: The Ultimate Data Structures Cheat Sheet
articles.brief: Data structures are tools. Picking the right one depends on what operation you do most: lookup, insert, delete, ordered traversal, top-k, prefix search, or graph navigation. Start from operation frequency, not from habit.
articles.primaryConcept: The Ultimate Data Structures Cheat Sheet

articles.title: The Ultimate Guide to Acing the System Design Interview
articles.brief: System Design interviews are collaborative whiteboard sessions, not trick-question coding tests. Follow the framework — Requirements → Estimations → API → Data Model → High-Level Architecture → Deep-Dive — and you turn vague product ideas into defensible, production-ready designs.

articles.brief: When a single database server hits its limits, sharding and partitioning offer powerful strategies to scale.

articles.title: How to serve data at lightning speed | Caching Strategies (Redis/Memcached)
articles.brief: Master caching to accelerate data access, improve system responsiveness, and scale efficiently.
